COPYRIGHT IN USEFUL ARTICLES — THE SEPARABILITY RULE (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 113; STAR ATHLETICA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Bay Lantern Studio, LLC · A table lamp with a cast figurative base and an etched pattern on the shade

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS USEFUL ARTICLE SEPARABILITY INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the rule of federal copyright law that governs the design of a useful article — a chair, a lamp, a garment, a bottle, a tool, a piece of machinery, or any other object with an intrinsic utilitarian function. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes for Bay Lantern Studio, LLC concerning A table lamp with a cast figurative base and an etched pattern on the shade. Copyright protects original works of authorship, including pictorial, graphic, and sculptural works, but 17 U.S.C. § 101 provides that the design of a useful article is a pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work only if, and only to the extent that, the design incorporates features that can be identified separately from, and are capable of existing independently of, the utilitarian aspects of the article. Courts call that inquiry separability. In Star Athletica, L.L.C. v. Varsity Brands, Inc., 580 U.S. 405 (2017), the Supreme Court stated a two-part test for it, abandoned the older distinction between physical and conceptual separability, and rejected tests that turned on the designer's intent or on the marketability of the feature. This Information Sheet states what 17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, and 113 provide and what the Supreme Court and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, whose decisions bind the federal district courts in California, have said about those provisions. It is not a copyright application, not a registration, not a demand letter, not a court filing, not an assessment of whether copyright protects any feature of A table lamp with a cast figurative base and an etched pattern on the shade, and not legal advice.

HOW THIS INFORMATION SHEET RELATES TO THIS PROJECT'S OTHER INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY DOCUMENTS
Separability is a question of copyrightable subject matter, and this Information Sheet does not restate the other copyright and design-protection subjects that this project addresses in separate documents. The general limits on copyrightable subject matter — the 17 U.S.C. § 102(b) exclusions, originality, the idea/expression and fact/expression distinctions, merger, and scenes a faire — are the subject of this project's document on what copyright does not protect, which expressly leaves the useful article doctrine to a separate document. Registration with the Copyright Office and the precondition it places on an infringement suit are the subject of this project's copyright registration document. Fair use, the first sale doctrine, joint authorship, copyright preemption of state-law claims, and the federal and California moral rights statutes for works of visual art are each the subject of separate documents. Protection for the appearance of a product under other bodies of law is addressed elsewhere as well: design patents in this project's design patent document, product configuration and packaging in its trade dress document, and semiconductor chip designs in its mask work document. This Information Sheet concerning A table lamp with a cast figurative base and an etched pattern on the shade addresses only whether, and to what extent, copyright reaches the design of a useful article.

THE STATUTORY FRAMEWORK: PICTORIAL, GRAPHIC, AND SCULPTURAL WORKS AND THE SEPARABILITY PROVISO
17 U.S.C. § 102(a) provides that copyright protection subsists in original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression, and lists eight categories of works of authorship; § 102(a)(5) names pictorial, graphic, and sculptural works. Section 101 defines that category to include two-dimensional and three-dimensional works of fine, graphic, and applied art, photographs, prints and art reproductions, maps, globes, charts, diagrams, models, and technical drawings, including architectural plans. The same definition adds two further sentences that do the work in every useful article case. The first states that such works include works of artistic craftsmanship insofar as their form but not their mechanical or utilitarian aspects are concerned. The second states that the design of a useful article is considered a pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work only if, and only to the extent that, the design incorporates pictorial, graphic, or sculptural features that can be identified separately from, and are capable of existing independently of, the utilitarian aspects of the article. Two textual features of that proviso recur throughout the case law: the phrase "only if, and only to the extent that" addresses both whether any part of the design is protected and how much of it is, and the two conditions that follow — separate identification and independent existence — are stated together, so that a feature satisfying only one of them is not protected.

WHAT COUNTS AS A USEFUL ARTICLE, AND WHY THE ARTICLE ITSELF IS NEVER THE PROTECTED WORK
17 U.S.C. § 101 defines a useful article as an article having an intrinsic utilitarian function that is not merely to portray the appearance of the article or to convey information, and adds that an article that is normally a part of a useful article is itself considered a useful article. The definition therefore turns on function rather than on price, craftsmanship, or artistic ambition: an object whose only function is to portray its own appearance or to convey information — a painting, a photograph, a map, a chart — is not a useful article at all, while a lamp, a belt buckle, a bicycle rack, or a mannequin is, and so is a component that is normally part of one. In Star Athletica the Supreme Court restated the consequence of that definition in a single sentence: the statute does not protect useful articles as such. What may be protected is a pictorial, graphic, or sculptural feature incorporated into the article's design, and then only to the extent the separability conditions are met. The Court added a corollary that runs in the other direction: copying a useful article into another medium does not create rights in the article, because although a replica such as a cardboard model of a car may itself be copyrightable, it gives rise to no rights in the useful article that inspired it.

THE STAR ATHLETICA TWO-PART TEST: SEPARATE IDENTIFICATION AND INDEPENDENT EXISTENCE
In Star Athletica, L.L.C. v. Varsity Brands, Inc., 580 U.S. 405 (2017), the Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve widespread disagreement over the proper test for the separate-identification and independent-existence requirements of 17 U.S.C. § 101, and held that an artistic feature of the design of a useful article is eligible for copyright protection if the feature can be perceived as a two- or three-dimensional work of art separate from the useful article and would qualify as a protectable pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work either on its own or in some other medium if imagined separately from the useful article. The Court described the first requirement as not onerous: the decisionmaker need only look at the article and spot an element that appears to have pictorial, graphic, or sculptural qualities. The second requirement is the harder one; it asks whether the separately identified feature has the capacity to exist apart from the utilitarian aspects of the article, and a feature that cannot exist as a pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work once separated was never a pictorial, graphic, or sculptural feature at all but rather one of the article's utilitarian aspects. The Court summarized the inquiry as a counterfactual: whether the feature would have been eligible for protection had it originally been fixed in a medium other than the useful article before being applied to it. Applying that test, the Court held that the arrangements of lines, chevrons, and colorful shapes on the surface of the respondents' cheerleading uniforms satisfied both requirements.

THE PHYSICAL VERSUS CONCEPTUAL SEPARABILITY DISTINCTION IS NO LONGER USED
Before Star Athletica, many courts and commentators divided separability into two kinds drawn from the 1976 Act's legislative history: physical separability, where the feature could be physically removed from the article by ordinary means while leaving the article's utilitarian aspects intact, and conceptual separability, applied where the feature could not be physically removed. The Supreme Court rejected the premise on which that division rested. It held that the statute does not require the useful article to remain after the artistic feature has been imaginatively separated from it, because separability is a conceptual undertaking directed at the feature rather than at the remainder of the object, and it reasoned that requiring the article to survive intact would effectively abrogate the rule of Mazer v. Stein and read the words "applied art" out of the statute. Having rejected that requirement, the Court stated that it necessarily abandoned the physical/conceptual distinction, noting that the lower courts had been unable to agree on any single conceptual separability test.

WHAT A SEPARABLE FEATURE PROTECTS: NOT THE SHAPE, CUT, OR DIMENSIONS OF THE ARTICLE
Star Athletica describes the consequence of a finding of separability as narrowly as it describes the test. The Court stated that even if the respondents ultimately established a valid copyright in the surface decorations of their cheerleading uniforms, they would have no right to prohibit anyone from manufacturing a uniform of identical shape, cut, and dimensions, and could prohibit only the reproduction of the surface designs in any tangible medium of expression. Answering the objection that its approach would let copyright reach industrial design generally, the Court added that its test does not render the shape, cut, and physical dimensions of the uniforms eligible for copyright protection. The Court also rejected the argument that a two-dimensional design fails the test because, once imaginatively removed, it retains the outline of the article it was applied to: two-dimensional applied art correlates to the contours of the article on which it is applied in the same way that fine art corresponds to the shape of its canvas, and a design etched on a guitar and moved to an album cover does not replicate the guitar as a useful article.

CONSIDERATIONS THE SUPREME COURT REFUSED TO BUILD INTO THE TEST
The petitioner in Star Athletica asked the Supreme Court to add two objective components to the separability analysis: whether the design elements reflect the designer's artistic judgment exercised independently of functional influence, and whether the feature would still be marketable to a significant segment of the community without its utilitarian function. The Court rejected both because neither is grounded in the text of the statute. As to the first, the Court explained that the statutory inquiry is limited to how the article and the feature are perceived, not how or why they were designed, so evidence of the creator's design methods, purposes, and reasons is beside the point. As to the second, the Court said that nothing in the statute suggests that copyrightability depends on market surveys, and that asking whether some segment of the market would be interested in a work threatens to prize popular art over other forms or to substitute judicial aesthetic preferences for the policy choices Congress made — citing the rule of Bleistein v. Donaldson Lithographing Co., 188 U.S. 239 (1903), against judicial evaluation of artistic merit.

SECTION 113: REPRODUCING A WORK ON A USEFUL ARTICLE, PORTRAYING A USEFUL ARTICLE, AND PHOTOGRAPHS IN ADVERTISING
17 U.S.C. § 113 states three rules that surround the separability proviso. Subsection (a) provides that the exclusive right to reproduce a pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work in copies includes the right to reproduce the work in or on any kind of article, whether useful or otherwise; the Supreme Court described § 101 as the mirror image of § 113(a), because § 113(a) protects a work first fixed in some medium other than a useful article and later applied to one, while § 101 addresses art first fixed in the medium of a useful article. Subsection (b) provides that Title 17 affords the owner of copyright in a work that portrays a useful article as such no greater or lesser rights over the making, distribution, or display of the useful article portrayed than the law in effect on December 31, 1977 afforded; the practical effect, long recognized, is that a copyright in a drawing or photograph of an object does not control the manufacture of the object depicted. Subsection (c) provides that where a work has been lawfully reproduced in useful articles offered for sale or other distribution to the public, copyright does not include any right to prevent the making, distribution, or display of pictures or photographs of those articles in connection with advertisements or commentaries related to their distribution or display, or in connection with news reports.

MASS PRODUCTION AND INDUSTRIAL USE DO NOT DEFEAT COPYRIGHT IN THE ARTISTIC FEATURE
The foundation of the modern rule is Mazer v. Stein, 347 U.S. 201 (1954), which concerned statuettes of dancing figures that the copyright owners made and sold as lamp bases. The Supreme Court held that the copyright in the statuettes was not lost or invalidated because the works were intended for, and used in, mass-produced articles of commerce. The Court found nothing in the copyright statute supporting the argument that the intended use or use in industry of an article eligible for copyright bars or invalidates its registration, and declined to read such a limitation into the copyright law. The Court framed the relationship between copyright and design patent in the same passage: the dichotomy of protection for the aesthetic is not beauty and utility but art for the copyright and the invention of original and ornamental design for design patents. Star Athletica treated Mazer as controlling background, reasoning that a rule denying protection to features that play any role in an article's function would effectively abrogate Mazer and read applied art out of the statute.

Subsection (c) provides that where a work has been lawfully reproduced in useful articles offered for sale or other distribution to the public, copyright does not include any right to prevent the making, distribution, or display of pictures or photographs of those articles in connection with advertisements or commentaries related to their distribution or display, or in connection with news reports.

expectedJSON.body: The foundation of the modern rule is Mazer v. Stein, 347 U.S. 201 (1954), which concerned statuettes of dancing figures that the copyright owners made and sold as lamp bases. The Supreme Court held that the copyright in the statuettes was not lost or invalidated because the works were intended for, and used in, mass-produced articles of commerce. The Court found nothing in the copyright statute supporting the argument that the intended use or use in industry of an article eligible for copyright bars or invalidates its registration, and declined to read such a limitation into the copyright law. The Court framed the relationship between copyright and design patent in the same passage: the dichotomy of protection for the aesthetic is not beauty and utility but art for the copyright and the invention of original and ornamental design for design patents. Star Athletica treated Mazer as controlling background, reasoning that a rule denying protection to features that play any role in an article's function would effectively abrogate Mazer and read applied art out of the statute.

expectedJSON.body: Copyright is not the only federal regime that reaches the appearance of a manufactured object, and Star Athletica opened by observing that Congress has provided copyright protection for original works of art but not for industrial designs. Under 35 U.S.C. § 171(a), a person who invents a new, original, and ornamental design for an article of manufacture may obtain a design patent, subject to the conditions and requirements of Title 35. The Supreme Court noted in Star Athletica that design patent and copyright are not mutually exclusive, and it declined to adopt a presumption against copyright protection for industrial design drawn from Congress's repeated failure to enact general industrial design legislation. Congress has instead legislated for particular articles: 17 U.S.C. §§ 901-914 protect semiconductor chip mask works, and chapter 13 of Title 17 creates a separate, registration-based regime for original designs of useful articles that make the article attractive or distinctive in appearance to the purchasing or using public, which 17 U.S.C. § 1301(a)(2) limits in practice to vessel hulls, decks, and combinations of the two, including plugs and molds.

expectedJSON.body: Federal district courts in California follow decisions of the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which has applied the separability rule to the shape of containers. In Inhale, Inc. v. Starbuzz Tobacco, Inc., 755 F.3d 1038 (9th Cir. 2014), the copyright owner claimed protection for the distinctive shape of a hookah water container and argued that distinctiveness of shape made the shape separable from the container's function. The court of appeals rejected the argument. It noted that in Ets-Hokin v. Skyy Spirits, Inc., 225 F.3d 1068 (9th Cir. 2000), it had held that the shape of a vodka bottle without a distinctive shape was not conceptually separable, and it found persuasive the Copyright Office's determination, expressed in an opinion letter and an internal manual, that whether an item's shape is distinctive does not affect separability. The court held that the shape of a container is not independent of the container's utilitarian function of holding the contents within its shape insofar as the shape accomplishes that function, and summarized its holding as covering any part of a container that merely accomplishes the containing. The court was careful to say that it did not suggest that no element of a container could ever be identified separately from and exist independently of the container, and it noted that the plaintiff had not argued that imagery on the container was separable.
